summary: In Greek mythology, Acamas or Akamas (Ancient Greek Ἀκάμας) son of Eussorus (Eüssorus) is the Thracian co-captain who, with Peirous son of Imbrasus, leads the Thracians enclosed by the Hellespont to Troy. Homer has Agamemnon kill him early in Iliad Book 6. Distinct from Antenor's Trojan son and from Theseus' Athenian Acamas.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἀκάμας; Homer identifies this warrior by the patronymic "son of Eussorus."

sections.heading: Thracian captain
paragraphs: In the Catalogue of Ships Acamas and Peirous lead the Thracians whom the strong stream of the Hellespont encloses (Iliad 2.844–845). Apollodorus lists Acamas son of Eusorus among the allies who came to join the Trojans.

At the opening of Book 6 Agamemnon first breaks a Trojan battalion and smites Eussorus' son Acamas — a tall, valiant man — driving his spear through the crest into the forehead until darkness covers his eyes. Later handbook notices sometimes attribute his death to Ajax or Idomeneus; Homer's named slayer is Agamemnon.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id acamas-thracian is the Hellespontine Thracian alone. Not acamas-antenorid (Antenor's Dardanian son), not acamas-athens (Theseus' prince), and not the Dulichian suitor.
